tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark, RunBenchmark.py public, Intel Core i7-12700H stated) times CharLS via pillow-jpls against Pillow's WebP lossless (libwebp), PNG (zlib) and JPEG 2000 (OpenJPEG) plugins; the CharLS wheel's compiler and flags are not stated, so not A.

corrections.baseline: WebP lossless via Pillow 10.1.0 (libwebp, quality=100, method 1 and 5), Pillow PNG plugin (zlib, not libpng) and Pillow JPEG 2000 plugin (OpenJPEG), all run in-process in Image-Compression-Benchmark; the CharLS README separately cites the original HP JPEG-LS code, JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000
corrections.claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark, CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB; times in seconds, measured with time.time() in RunBenchmark.py): JPEG-LS (CharLS via pillow-jpls) compress 72.237 / decompress 66.567, size 1931584595 bytes. Versus WebP lossless m1 (libwebp) 720.160 / 37.044, 1496478650 bytes: about 10.0x faster compression but 1.8x slower decompression and 29% larger output (derived from page data); versus WebP lossless m5 1112.134 / 49.442: 15.4x faster compression, 1.35x slower decompression (derived from page data). Versus Pillow PNG (optimize=False, zlib) 334.791 / 33.677: 4.6x faster compression, about 2x slower decompression, slightly smaller output. Versus Pillow JPEG2000 (OpenJPEG) 319.912 / 275.398: 4.4x and 4.1x faster (derived from page data). CharLS README: 'about twice as fast as the original HP code, and beats both JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000 by a factor 3' (cites imagecompression.info, not opened).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Python 3.9, Pillow 10.1.0, pillow-jpls 1.3.2 wheel (links CharLS 2.4.2 statically via Conan per its conanfile.txt); wheel compiler and flags not stated
corrections.caveats: The page does compare against a listed baseline: Pillow's WebP plugin is libwebp. Against it CharLS wins only on encode (about 10x vs WebP lossless with quality=100, which is libwebp's maximum-effort lossless setting) and loses on decode (1.8x slower) and ratio (29% larger). Pillow's PNG codec uses zlib directly rather than libpng, and Pillow's JPEG 2000 plugin is OpenJPEG. All Pillow-based rows (PNG, WebP, JPEG 2000, JPEG-LS) run in-process through exec() with the same PNM read/write overhead, so they are comparable to each other, while EXE-based codecs include per-file process startup. JPEG-XL -e1 (43.0 s / 57.7 s, smaller files) and QOI/fNBLI beat JPEG-LS on the same table, so CharLS is not the fastest lossless codec here. The README's 'twice as fast as HP code' claim rests on an unopened, dated imagecompression.info page. The 'JPEG-LS-ext' row is a different codec (ImCvt) and is not counted.

notes: Numbers match the CLIC2021 table exactly; units confirmed as seconds from RunBenchmark.py. The record's caveat that no listed baseline is compared was wrong (libwebp via Pillow), so baseline_in_list is now true, but the win over libwebp is encode-only. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 224 stars, last commit 2026-10-02 (dependabot), GDCM listed as a user in the README.

tier_reason: Third-party measurement by the Wuffs author against Debian's libpng16 with public harness code (google/wuffs v0.3.0-beta.1 test/c/std/png.c and test/c/mimiclib/png.c), gcc -O3 and clang 9/gcc 10, on an Intel Core m3-6Y30, plus independent numbers in mango's examples/image/png_benchmark; not raised to A because the libspng commit measured is not pinned and the harness notes libspng 0.6.2 skipped Adler-32 verification (inverted-flag bug fixed in commit 9c35dc3), so equal work against libpng is not assured.

corrections.hardware: Intel Core m3-6Y30 @ 0.90GHz (Skylake laptop, x86_64) for the Wuffs blog numbers; Intel Core i7-11800H for the mango README numbers
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 9 and gcc 10 with -O3 -DWUFFS_MIMIC (blog Reproduction section: gcc -O3 test/c/std/png.c -DWUFFS_MIMIC -lm -lpng -lz); libspng spng.c is #included into the harness translation unit; libpng is Debian Bullseye's packaged libpng16.so
corrections.claimed_speedup: Wuffs blog appendix (third-party, MB/s of decoded output, libpng = 1.00x): libspng with checksum verification decodes 1.02x to 1.07x faster on the 19k, 40k, 77k and 4002k images (e.g. 4002k_24bpp 110 MB/s clang9 vs 104 MB/s) and 1.39x (clang9, 203 MB/s) / 1.33x (gcc10, 194 MB/s) on 552k_32bpp_verify_checksum vs libpng 146 MB/s; the blog's best ratio, 1.62x (236 MB/s, 552k_32bpp_ignore_checksum/clang9), compares checksum-skipping libspng against libpng, which cannot skip checksums. mango README (i7-11800H, 2560x1600 image): spng decode 37.7 ms vs libpng 57.3 ms (1.52x) and encode 215.9 ms vs 820.5 ms (3.8x); 4833x5875 image: decode 296.6 ms vs 379.5 ms (1.28x), encode 2424.7 ms vs 14051.3 ms (5.8x) (ratios derived from page data). libspng README: 'outperforms the reference implementation in common use cases' with a chart image only.
corrections.caveats: Decode gains over libpng are modest and image-dependent (1.02x to 1.07x on four of five Wuffs test images). Wuffs' mimiclib notes that libspng 0.6.2 did not verify Adler-32 (an inverted SPNG_CTX_IGNORE_ADLER32 check, fixed in commit 9c35dc3, Dec 2020) and never verifies the final IDAT chunk's CRC-32; the blog does not pin the libspng commit, so the small gains may partly reflect skipped verification. In mango's png_benchmark.cpp the spng decoder is set to SPNG_CRC_USE (CRC errors ignored) while libpng uses defaults, and the spng encoder uses compression level 3 with the Up filter only while libpng uses default settings, so spng's 3.8x to 5.8x encode lead comes with 14% to 21% larger files (3232 vs 2843 KB; 34083 vs 28180 KB). The same blog shows libpng with zlib-ng is 1.01x to 1.21x faster than stock libpng, which narrows the gap. Code activity: the only 2026 commits are a copyright-year update; the previous commit is from 2023-12-20.

notes: All cited Wuffs and mango numbers are on the pages and belong to the libspng/spng rows. The record wrongly said the blog gives no CPU model (it names the Intel Core m3-6Y30 under Hardware); the tier stays B rather than A because of the Adler-32 verification bug in libspng 0.6.2 and the unpinned version. Metadata checked: BSD-2-Clause, 843 stars, last commit 2026-08-31 (copyright-year bump only).

tier_reason: First-party README table (repeated on the wiki home page) of GDAL end-to-end timings against OpenJPEG and Kakadu; benchmark/results.txt gives the gdal_translate commands and driver versions but only 'xx' placeholders, and no CPU model, compiler flags or public input images are given.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (16 threads, GDAL release build, Fedora 42; seconds), Grok (JP2Grok) vs Kakadu (JP2KAK) vs OpenJPEG: Spot 6 (Network Storage) 35.17 vs 344 vs 85; Spot 6 (Local Storage) 26.92 vs 30.57 vs 52.09; Pleiades (Region) 0.74 vs 1.41 vs 4.28. Versus OpenJPEG that is 2.4x, 1.9x and 5.8x faster (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: JPEG 2000 is outside the listed baselines (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif); OpenJPEG is the recognizable open-source incumbent. First-party end-to-end GDAL timings that include I/O, caching and region reads, not codec-only throughput. benchmark/results.txt describes the method (gdal_translate on a 26kx26k 12-bit Spot 6 image with 2kx2k tiles, with and without TLM markers; network case is MinIO with 50 ms latency and VSI_CACHE=YES; drivers Grok 20.0, OpenJPEG 2.5.4, Kakadu 8.4) but its result slots are 'xx' placeholders, so the README numbers cannot be tied to a recorded run; CPU model, compiler flags and the input images are not published. Kakadu's 344 s network-storage time versus 30.57 s locally suggests an I/O-pattern effect rather than codec speed (inference). AGPL-3.0-only (LICENSE says version 3, no 'or later'), a strong copyleft licence for anyone embedding it.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; no independent Grok vs OpenJPEG measurement was reachable (encode.su and fastcompression.com are egress-blocked). Licence AGPL-3.0-only confirmed from the LICENSE header; 295 stars, last commit 2026-10-03, not archived or a fork.
